raw_text:
Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is a catheter-based strategy to reduce thromboembolism in atrial fibrillation (AF) by excluding the dominant site of atrial thrombus formation. The rationale is anatomically and pathophysiologically strong: in nonvalvular AF, most cardiac thrombi arise in the left atrial appendage (LAA), a trabeculated, contractile cul-de-sac whose stasis, endothelial dysfunction, and complex morphology promote thrombogenesis [1], [2]. Oral anticoagulation remains the standard for stroke prevention, and direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) improved safety and convenience compared with warfarin in major trials [3], [4], [5], [6]. Nevertheless, bleeding, frailty, renal dysfunction, drug interactions, nonadherence, and recurrent hemorrhage leave an important population in whom a mechanical alternative is attractive.

Early human experience with endocardial LAA occlusion began with the PLAATO device, establishing procedural feasibility but also highlighting pericardial effusion and device-related complications as central safety issues [7], [8]. The field matured with the WATCHMAN program. In PROTECT AF, LAAC was noninferior to warfarin for a composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death, but early procedural complications were more frequent [9]. Subsequent analyses showed a learning-curve effect, with lower serious pericardial effusion and procedural event rates in continued-access experience [10]. Residual peri-device flow was common, although early PROTECT AF substudy data did not show a clear association with thromboembolism, a question later revisited in larger registries [11].

Longer follow-up strengthened the evidence base. PROTECT AF extended follow-up suggested reductions in hemorrhagic stroke, cardiovascular mortality, and all-cause mortality compared with warfarin [12]. The ASAP study supported the feasibility of WATCHMAN implantation in patients considered unsuitable for warfarin, using antiplatelet-based therapy after implantation [13]. PREVAIL, designed with more contemporary operators and stricter safety endpoints, did not meet all efficacy noninferiority criteria but demonstrated improved procedural safety and low late ischemic event rates [14]. Patient-level meta-analysis of PROTECT AF and PREVAIL confirmed broadly similar protection from ischemic events, less hemorrhagic stroke, and more early procedural risk with LAAC [15]. In post-approval practice, procedural success was high and complication rates were lower than in the initial randomized trial era, reflecting device iteration, imaging, and operator experience [16], [17].

Large registries have been crucial because LAAC candidates are often older and sicker than randomized-trial participants. EWOLUTION showed high implant success with WATCHMAN and acceptable one-year stroke and bleeding outcomes in a population with frequent anticoagulation contraindications [18], [19]. Device-related thrombus (DRT), however, remains a clinically important late complication. In pooled WATCHMAN trial data, DRT occurred in a minority of patients but was associated with increased ischemic events, supporting systematic surveillance imaging and individualized antithrombotic therapy [20]. Preprocedural computed tomography and transesophageal echocardiography improve understanding of LAA ostial dimensions, landing zone, depth, lobar anatomy, and adjacent structures, thereby reducing sizing errors and helping anticipate leaks or embolization risk [21].

Other endocardial devices expanded the field. The Amplatzer Cardiac Plug and later Amulet use a lobe-and-disc design that can seal short or complex appendages and allow immediate ostial coverage [22], [23]. Prospective Amulet observational data showed high procedural success, although periprocedural complications and DRT required ongoing vigilance [24]. In the randomized Amulet IDE trial, Amulet was noninferior to WATCHMAN for safety and effectiveness and achieved higher rates of complete LAA occlusion, at the cost of somewhat more procedure-related complications in early experience [25]. The PRAGUE-17 trial directly compared LAAC with DOACs in high-risk AF and found LAAC noninferior for a composite of stroke, systemic embolism, cardiovascular death, major bleeding, and procedure/device complications, supporting its role beyond warfarin-ineligible patients when bleeding risk is high [26]. Next-generation WATCHMAN FLX, evaluated in PINNACLE FLX, improved conformability, recapturability, and sealing, with high implant success and low early serious adverse event rates [27]. The NCDR LAAO Registry has since provided real-world benchmarking for patient selection, procedural safety, and quality improvement [28].

Procedure planning begins with confirming nonvalvular AF, estimating thromboembolic and bleeding risk, excluding active LAA thrombus, and clarifying whether the goal is avoidance of long-term anticoagulation or reduction of recurrent bleeding. Most procedures are performed under transesophageal or intracardiac echocardiographic guidance with transseptal puncture, heparinization, angiography, device sizing, stability testing, and confirmation of seal before release. Post-implant antithrombotic regimens vary: warfarin or DOAC plus aspirin, dual antiplatelet therapy, or single antiplatelet therapy may be chosen according to bleeding risk, device type, and imaging findings. Follow-up imaging, commonly at 45–90 days, assesses leak and DRT.

Epicardial suture ligation with the LARIAT system represents a different percutaneous concept, excluding the LAA without an intracardiac implant. Early series demonstrated feasibility but raised concerns about pericarditis, effusion, laceration, and the need for both endocardial and epicardial access [29], [30]. Thus, its use has been more selective than endocardial occluders.

Overall, percutaneous LAAC is best viewed not as a universal replacement for anticoagulation but as an evidence-based alternative for carefully selected AF patients at high stroke risk and unacceptable long-term anticoagulant burden. Future priorities include randomized comparisons with contemporary DOAC strategies, optimal post-implant antithrombotic regimens, management of DRT and peri-device leak, and broader evaluation in underrepresented groups such as advanced chronic kidney disease, extreme frailty, and prior intracranial hemorrhage.
